..
KEY MESSAGE 1...
A renewed push of moisture is forecast today in strengthening
south/southwest flow. This is occurring ahead of a shortwave
trough that is riding up the Ohio Valley and will cross our
region during the late afternoon and evening. Expected
precipitable water values of 1.8 to 2.0 inches during this
period represent values above the 98th percentile areawide. With
initial high clouds providing only modest hindrance to heating,
no capping of note on model soundings, and increasing support 
for lift from warm advection and the approaching wave, CAMs 
suggest that scattered showers and thunderstorms may begin to 
fire during the late morning and early afternoon hours. The 
environment will already be supportive of warm rain processes at
that point given the increasing PWAT, increasingly saturated 
column, and rising warm cloud depths.

As the afternoon wears on, these factors continue to improve, 
and a more robust shield of rain and embedded thunderstorms is 
likely as the shortwave approaches. Areas east of Pittsburgh 
may see enhanced low-level convergence as strengthening 
south/southwest flow butts up against southeast flow just to our
east as surface high pressure moves further away from the New 
England coast. This could locally enhance rainfall rates to
concerning levels. HREF probabilities of greater than 1" are
generally 60 to 90 percent in the previous Flood Watch areas,
with maximum 24-hour rainfall totals ending at 06Z Sunday 
showing several 3-5" bullseyes. 24-hour LPPM values of 2-4" 
focus especially on areas northeast of Pittsburgh. Such totals 
represent the high-end scenario, but the environment is 
certainly capable of supporting them. While these areas have the
highest risk of flooding, elected to expand the Flood Watch to 
the rest of the CWA. Much of the CWA has soil moisture levels in
excess of 50 percent according to MRMS, including portions of 
eastern OH/northwest PA not previously covered by the Watch. 
Although low-level forcing may not be as robust as areas to the 
east, the same favorable environmental parameters for heavy rain
(high PWAT/saturated soundings/etc) are present, and at least 
isolated flooding issues are possible. WPC has expanded the 
Slight Risk for excessive rainfall to virtually all of the 
forecast area.

In addition to the flooding threat, a window for strong to
isolated severe thunderstorms exists. Joint 10km neighborhood 
probabilities of 1000 J/kg of SBCAPE and 30 knots of 0-6km shear
reach the 60-80 percent level across much of the area during 
the noon to 6 PM period. While mid- level lapse rates will be 
poor and soundings eventually lead to tall and skinny CAPE 
profiles, there may be enough storm organization and steep low- 
level lapse rates to produce damaging wind potential, with 
small-scale bowing structures possible. Even a tornado cannot be
totally ruled out, thanks to the low-level southeast flow noted
above allowing for backed surface winds. 

The heavy rain threat should begin to wane during the late
evening/midnight period as the shortwave crosses, leaving some
scattered showers in its wake. Lingering low-level moisture
should lead to abundant stratus coverage by Sunday morning.

KEY MESSAGE 2...
Another severe storm threat could emerge on Sunday, as 
developing Great Lakes troughing drops a surface cold front into
our region during the late afternoon and evening hours. The 
trough will provide sufficient deep shear on the order of 35-45 
knots, with higher values closer to the lakes. Moisture 
certainly remains present with surface dewpoints remaining in 
the upper 60s to around 70. However, there remains some question
as to the level of clearing and thus destabilization that can 
take place, as ensembles continue to suggest a range of sky 
cover outcomes. This results in 25th/75th percentile SBCAPE 
spreads of below 500 J/kg to above 1100-1200 J/kg. Also, the 
subsident warm layer at 800mb noted by the previous shift 
continues to show up in some HREF members, but not the RRFS. 
Thus, uncertainty in the level of severe threat continues. 
However, the front and the level of shear do suggest that even 
lower-end CAPE levels may not be sufficient to totally suppress 
convection, and some CAMs do show at least widely scattered 
storm coverage during frontal passage. Given the shear, any 
storm will be capable of marginally severe wind and hail 
threats. A more widespread threat could emerge if later runs 
show better potential for destabilization and a lack of capping.

KEY MESSAGE 3... 
Minor timing issues remain, but the trough axis is still slated
to cross the region at some point Monday. At least scattered
showers will likely linger through Sunday night and perhaps into
Monday morning, before mid-level ridging provides a dry
interlude by Monday afternoon. This break may last until 
Tuesday night or Wednesday, depending on the progress of the 
next front.
